analysis.one_liner: Replaces state product-liability laws with uniform federal rules that make it harder for people injured by defective products to sue and win.
analysis.headline: With 62 cosponsors from both parties, the bill was referred to two House committees in June 1989 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out each state's own product-liability rules and replaced them with one federal set of standards for lawsuits over injuries caused by defective products. It would give manufacturers a new defense for dangerous designs, cut the time injured people have to sue to two years, sharply limit punitive damages (especially against drug and device makers), and reduce jury awards by any workers' compensation the injured person received. It also included a few protections for people hurt by products: a presumption of liability for makers of firefighting gear that fails federal standards, and rules letting courts share evidence of hidden product dangers with other victims and federal agencies instead of letting it be sealed away.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and product sellers gain the most: a new 'state-of-the-art' defense for dangerous designs, an end to strict liability for retailers, a two-year deadline for lawsuits, a full defense when the injured person was more than half at fault due to alcohol or unprescribed drugs, reduced awards for anyone receiving workers' compensation, and near-impossible standards for punitive damages against drug and medical device makers. Product liability insurers gain from fewer and smaller claims. Firefighters gain a presumption that manufacturers of non-compliant protective gear are liable for their injuries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufacturers, drug and device makers, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Gives firefighters a presumption that makers of firefighting equipment or protective clothing are liable for their injuries if the gear did not meet OSHA fire brigade standards or a stricter state standard.

Allows courts to disclose information about unreasonable product risks to other claimants with identical defect claims and to federal agencies investigating the defect, despite confidentiality limits.

Bars settlements or court orders from forcing claimants to destroy or return documents (unless the defendant agrees to preserve them), and prohibits agreements that stop an attorney from representing other claimants against the same defendant.
Keeps product sellers liable as if they were the manufacturer when the manufacturer cannot be served or a judgment against it could not be enforced.
Carves out asbestos claims and environmental and pollution claims from the bill entirely, leaving existing law in place.

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products would face a two-year filing deadline from discovery, damages reduced by any workers' compensation received, a complete bar on recovery if they were more than 50 percent at fault because of alcohol or unprescribed drugs, and far higher hurdles for punitive damages — nearly insurmountable against drug and device makers. Workers hurt on the job would lose the most, since their awards are offset and employers lose most subrogation leverage. State legislatures and courts would lose control over their own tort law.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a two-year statute of limitations running from when a person discovered (or should have discovered) the harm and its cause, superseding any longer state deadline — a short window for latent injuries.

Punitive damages against drug and medical device manufacturers would be allowed only if the claimant proves, by clear and convincing evidence, that the company intentionally withheld or misrepresented required safety information to the FDA or committed fraud — a near-prohibitive standard even where a company concealed known risks.
Any damages award would be reduced by the amount of workers' compensation the injured worker receives or is entitled to, cutting recovery for on-the-job injuries.
A claimant who was more than 50 percent at fault for the accident because of intoxication by alcohol or a non-prescribed drug would have no claim at all, regardless of how dangerous the product was.

The bill adds a 'state-of-the-art' defense letting manufacturers escape design liability by showing no feasible safer design existed at the time, superseding state law that may hold them to a higher duty.

Supporters would argue uniform federal rules cut litigation costs, reduce unpredictable jury awards, and lower product liability insurance premiums that get built into consumer prices; the bill itself requires ten years of Commerce Department reports on those insurance effects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a handful of genuinely pro-claimant provisions — the firefighter liability presumption, rules against burying evidence of product dangers in sealed settlements, and keeping sellers liable when the manufacturer is unreachable. But its center of gravity runs the other way: shorter deadlines, reduced awards, a near-total punitive damages shield for drug and device makers, and federal preemption of state consumer protections. On balance, the bill shifts the cost of dangerous products from the companies that make them to the people they injure, and the modest transparency provisions do not offset that.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees within a month, and never brought up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas A. Luken (D-OH) introduced the Product Liability Reform Act of 1989 on June 21, 1989, with three original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees.

On June 26 and July 17, 1989, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness.
Forty-four additional sponsors, most of them Republicans, signed on in July 1990, bringing total cosponsorship to 62 members — 17 Democrats and 45 Republicans.
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers and their families keep the full range of state-law remedies this bill would have trimmed, and states keep control of their own product-liability rules. Plaintiffs' attorneys keep the litigation practices the bill would have restricted; manufacturers, drug makers, and insurers forgo the liability limits they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers, who keep state-law remedies

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split across both parties — 17 of 257 House Democrats and 45 of 175 House Republicans — but the Democratic chairmen of both committees of referral never let it reach the floor.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of consumer and industrial products
industries.note: The bill gives manufacturers a state-of-the-art design defense, a two-year filing deadline, and reduced awards, shifting injury costs from producers to consumers. Its gain is directly the public's lost recourse.

Punitive damages would require clear and convincing proof of intentional fraud or misrepresentation to regulators — a shield even where a company concealed known safety risks. This is the bill's most industry-specific protection.

Fewer lawsuits and capped damages mean fewer and smaller claims against liability policies. The bill directs the Commerce Secretary to report for ten years on effects on insurance cost and availability, treating insurers as a principal stakeholder.

Sellers would no longer face strict liability — only negligence, breach of their own express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing — and would be relieved of any duty to inspect where none was reasonably possible.

industries.industry: Firefighting equipment and protective clothing manufacturers
industries.note: These makers face a presumption of liability for firefighter injuries when their gear fails OSHA fire brigade standards or a stricter state rule — the bill's clearest pro-claimant provision, aligned with worker safety.

Shorter deadlines, damage offsets, punitive damages hurdles, and mandatory mediation with cost-shifting would shrink the volume and value of product-liability cases. Its interest tracks injured consumers' access to court.
